articles.title: New Yankees Rumors on Jazz Chisholm Jr. Plans After 2B Does Not Receive Qualifying Contract Offer
articles.summary: Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s time on the New York Yankees reportedly could be coming to an end.
articles.body:
Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s time on the New York Yankees reportedly could be coming to an end.

After the American League East team did not offer him the $23.15 million qualifying offer on Monday, Yankees insider Jack Curry reported, "I think the Yankees are ready to part ways with Jazz Chisholm.

"… There was also inconsistency for his game this season, and I think for that $23 million, the Yankees weren't ready to go near that."

Curry suggested Anthony Volpe and José Caballero could take Chisholm's place at second base during the 2027 campaign if the starter does not return.

The Miami Marlins traded Chisholm to the Yankees during the 2024 campaign, and he was impressive in his first full season with the Bronx Bombers with 31 home runs, 80 RBI and 31 stolen bases in 2025.

The home run and RBI totals were career-high marks, and it also marked his second straight year with more than 30 stolen bases after he swiped 40 during the 2024 campaign.

Yet Chisholm saw a drop in production at the plate last season while slashing .231/.312/.399 with 19 home runs and 55 RBI. However, he stole a career-high 41 bases, proving his value in other ways even when his offense took a step back.

The biggest issue has been in the playoffs, as the second baseman hit .182 in each of the last two postseasons. Considering New York is often in World-Series-or-bust mode, that isn't good enough and has been a concern.

While the veteran is just 28 years old and will likely still be productive in 2027, it seems like the Yankees will look to use their resources elsewhere this offseason. Perhaps that means bringing in additional bullpen arms or even another major bat on the market.

But it seems like it will also mean the end of Chisholm's tenure with the team.

articles.title: Every MLB Team's Top Trade Assets in 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: In case anyone hasn't heard the hard truth, this MLB offseason doesn't feature a very good class of free agents. There's Tarik Skubal and then not much else.
articles.body:
In case anyone hasn't heard the hard truth, this MLB offseason doesn't feature a very good class of free agents. There's Tarik Skubal and then not much else.

On the plus side, this could make for a very active trade market.

For the sake of setting the stage, we're going to run through the best trade assets in every team's possession. These include specific players and more general areas of strength, such as major league surpluses and prospect riches.

With individual players, we've attempted to stay somewhere within reasonable boundaries. Would it be totally wild if, say, Bobby Witt Jr. hit the block this winter? You bet. But that idea and others face major headwinds.

We'll go division by division, starting in the American League East and ending in the National League West.

Prospect rankings are according to B/R's Joel Reuter .

The Orioles' infield logjam primarily concerns third base, which only has room for one starter between Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Coby Mayo and Jordan Westburg.

It's harder to imagine Gunnar Henderson or Jackson Holliday, though not necessarily because both should be untouchable. As unthinkable as it might have sounded once upon a time, neither has sky-high trade value right now.

Otherwise, there's no harm in other teams asking about Félix Bautista, Yennier Cano or Rico Garcia. Ryan Helsley is also worth asking about following his decision to opt in for 2027.

The Red Sox seem all but certain to trade Duran this winter, and not just because they stand to have an outfield logjam if they don't. He has more value than most guys coming off a 0.4-rWAR season, as he still has ample power and speed plus two remaining years of club control.

Triston Casas, Kristian Campbell and Brayan Bello are the former top prospects, and all three arguably need a change of scenery. With Casas, though, teams can wait and see if Boston non-tenders him.

The Yankees' major league rotation is so full that there aren't guaranteed roles for Luis Gil, Ryan Weathers or Clarke Schmidt going forward. They also have a couple intriguing prospects standing by, in Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange.

It's past time for the Yankees to look around for takers for Anthony Volpe and Jasson Domínguez. They were meant to be mainstays when they were brought up. That hasn't panned out, and the discourse around both has gotten a little too heated for comfort.

Rasmussen is in the No. 2 spot in MLB Trade Rumors' top 40 trade candidates for the winter. It's a little counter-intuitive, given that he was last seen serving as the ace for the American League champs. But the Rays are always budget-conscious, so Rasmussen's $20 million salary for 2027 represents a problem.

If the Rays would rather double-down on this year's success by buying on the trade market, they have six top-100 prospects in their system. Those include two shortstops and two catchers, so there's redundancy that could come into play.

Yeah, it's pretty bleak when it comes to Toronto's trade assets. Maybe they can get something for Andrés Giménez or Anthony Santander, yet rarely has the word "maybe" done such heavy lifting.

This is why selling high on guys should be in play, and we're specifically looking at Ernie Clement and Louis Varland. Clement is more of a nice guy to have than the All-Star starter he was this year. Varland had an elite year (1.27 ERA!) as the Jays' closer, but it's an outlier relative to the rest of his career.

The White Sox don't have an infield surplus right now, per se, but they are on a collision course with one.

Roch Cholowsky and Caleb Bonemer loom for the left side of the infield, so it might be worth their time to see what's out there for Miguel Vargas or Colson Montgomery.

As for the relievers, do they dare capitalize on Grant Taylor's breakout year and dangle him on the market? If it sounds crazy, just remember what the A's got when they cashed in Mason Miller in July 2025.

Chris Antonetti says Kwan is expected to be " a big part " of the 2027 team, but it remains fair game to speculate otherwise. He's due for free agency after next year, and he's thus in that window when the Guardians typically look to cash in when a player has trade value.

Given that each is due for a raise in arbitration, teams can try their luck calling about Jo Adell and Brayan Rocchio. After he failed to build on his 2025 breakout this year, Kyle Manzardo is also worth a spot on teams' radars.

Torkelson's name has popped up here and there in trade speculation in the past, and you can expect it to happen again this winter. He still has two years of club control left, but he could use a change of scenery that would hopefully involve a more power-friendly stadium than Comerica Park.

Torkelson obviously falls into the "former top prospect" bucket, but we're more so thinking about Colt Keith and Jace Jung. The latter just plain needs a change of scenery after failing to break through as a Tiger.

The Royals need some kind of dramatic pivot after back-to-back seasons of diminished returns, which is why Wacha needs to be on the market. He has one year left on his contract, and plenty of value after posting a 3.32 ERA over 200.2 innings.

It's right-handed bats that are in short supply across MLB, but the Royals might shop one or more of their lefties anyway. Vinnie Pasquantino could fetch a haul. Michael Massey and Kyle Isbel are worth less, but at least offer good gloves.

Even if he only has one 30-start season under his belt, Ryan is a two-time All-Star with established No. 2 upside. He's also only under club control for one more season, so now is the time if the Twins are ever going to trade him.

It's time for them to move on from leftover remnants of their last prospect wave. Royce Lewis should be put out there as a change of scenery candidate. Trevor Larnach is more of a known quantity, yet no longer a building block. He's 29 and headed into his final season under club control.

There were Langeliers trade rumors flying around for a minute during the summer, only for them to go quiet after he tore his meniscus . Teams are sure to check back in on the slugging catcher this winter, knowing full well that he's a Scott Boras client who is only two years from free agency.

Other trades the A's could make to restock their farm system could include Lawrence Butler or Zack Gelof, and maybe Brent Rooker if anyone out there still sees him as an impact hitter.

Speaking of Boras clients running short on club control, Peña is due for free agency after 2027. Houston's efforts to extend him have gone and still figure to go nowhere, so cashing in on the All-Star shortstop is looking like the smart play.

Paredes and Walker are sure to be discussed as well. Each offers reliable 25-homer power from the right side of the plate, an increasingly rare skill. Walker is also a four-time Gold Glover at first base. Both are slated for free agency after 2027.

At least among realistic targets, Neto is arguably the trade prize to be won this offseason. He's a 25-year-old with three straight seasons of 20-plus home runs and stolen bases under his belt, and his club control goes through 2029.

Detmers, meanwhile, is only a tier below Neto when it comes to trade value. He rather quietly posted a 3.36 ERA over 185.0 innings this season, and that was with a rock-solid 4.4 K/BB ratio. His club control runs through 2028.

The Mariners had six starters for five spots before they traded Luis Castillo in July, and now they're in the same spot after promoting Kade Anderson. George Kirby and Emerson Hancock are the obvious trade candidates, but don't rule out a Corbin Burnes-style deal for Logan Gilbert. He has one year before free agency.

The Mariners have seven top-100 prospects in their farm system, the most of any team in MLB. Even if Anderson (No. 7) and Ryan Sloan (No. 9) are off-limits, that still leaves five who could be centerpieces in a mega-trade.

It's been a minute since deGrom was the toast of baseball as a back-to-back Cy Young Award winner, but he's had two straight healthy seasons in which he mostly pitched effectively. He'd upgrade any staff in the game, so long as his prospective new team could get him to waive his no-trade clause.

Whereas deGrom has one year left on his contract, Seager is only halfway through his 10-year pact with the Rangers. It might nonetheless be now or never to trade him, as he's not getting any more durable and notably got worse at the plate this year. By way of 10-and-5 rights, he also has no-trade protection.

Ranking Freddy Peralta's Top Landing Spots 🛬

Ronald Acuña Jr. will draw a crowd if the Braves put him out there , but it might be wishful thinking for other teams. Even if the ground under his feet in Atlanta is shakier than it should be, the Braves would be selling low if they traded him now.

Albies and Murphy are post-prime players who could be eyed as change of scenery candidates. Jurickson Profar and Spencer Strider are more so buy-low types after lost seasons.

Profar is coming off a 162-game suspension, while Strider is now three years removed from his last season as a healthy and effective starting pitcher.

According to Barry Jackson of the Miami Herald , the Marlins are willing to listen on Lopez and Edwards. It'll take "a lot" for the team to part with either, and rightfully so. Each is a quality table-setter type of hitter, while Lopez is also a plus defender at shortstop. Both are controlled through 2029.

Assuming Sandy Alcantara is firmly off the table, the best pitchers Miami has to offer reside in the bullpen. Michael Petersen got some mentions as a summer trade candidate, and he should be on the block again after an unexpected age-32 breakout.

The Mets don't have a ton to barter with, but teams could be interested in taking fliers on Brett Baty and/or Mark Vientos. There's also Francisco Alvarez, who's still just 24 and a few years removed from being in the conversation as MLB's No. 1 prospect. He may yet emerge as an All-Star slugger at catcher.

Will there be any kind of market for Kodai Senga or Sean Manaea? Both struggled mightily in 2026, and they're due to make a combined $39 million in 2027. But if nothing else, both offer versatility as guys who could start or relieve as needed.

Yeah, definitely going out on a limb by citing Harper as a trade candidate here. But the Phillies do need to shake things up, and it's just never ideal when a star has a strained relationship with a president of baseball operations. If ever there was a time for Harper to be willing to waive his no-trade clause, it's now.

If the Phillies would prefer not to trade the two-time NL MVP, they might think about cutting down on redundancy in their farm system. Of their top five prospects for MLB Pipeline , three are shortstops: Aidan Miller, Bryan Rincon, Tyler Spangler.

The Nationals will probably get calls about James Wood, but Abrams is far more likely go actually go somewhere this winter. He has two years of club control left, and he's definitely a sell-high candidate after a 30-30, 5-rWAR season in 2026.

For his part, Young is more of a complementary piece for a contender than a cornerstone on a rebuilder like the Nationals. The Nats can market him as an ace defender who has a decent bat. He also has three years of club control left.

Because Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ are free agents, the Cubs might not be in a position to trade any hitters. But if they get into the trade market for starting pitching, they'll need to be prepared to part with Shaw and Ramírez. Both have appeal as recent top prospects who've had promising showings in the majors.

Shopping Edward Cabrera may sound pointless, but it might be a better idea than keeping him after he turned in a 5.96 ERA for the Cubs this season. The door should also be open on Justin Steele, who hasn't had a healthy season since 2023.

The Reds were willing to listen on De La Cruz during the summer, and that simply can't change this winter. They're not going to change Scott Boras' mind on an extension. And for a 30-30 shortstop with three years of club control left, teams would be more than happy to pay handsomely.

Or, the Reds could cash in some arms. Nick Lodolo and Andrew Abbott are worth asking about. So is Hunter Greene, albeit with the caveat that the flamethrower will miss all of 2027 after undergoing his second Tommy John surgery in August.

According to ESPN's Jeff Passan , the reigning World Series champions "will at least listen" on Megill, whereas Contreras "isn't going anywhere." They should nonetheless expect calls on both, given that each is only controlled through the 2027 season.

Given how in-demand righty hitters are, the Brewers should also field interest in Andrew Vaughn (who's also a free agent after 2027) and Joey Ortiz. The latter is more so about his glove, as he's shown he can play plus defense at both third base and shortstop.

The Pirates should field interest in Reynolds this winter. The dearth of good bats on the open market could make him extra valuable. And since he was a 1.3-rWAR player in 2025, there's logic in selling high after a bounceback year (featuring 40 doubles) and getting out of the second half of his eight-year contract.

Given how Paul Skenes struggled in 2026, the Bucs might be wary of offering up any starting pitchers. Still, Mitch Keller's contract would be better off elsewhere. The team also doesn't have a clear role for Carmen Mlodzinski, which was a point of contention during the season.

What do you do with a guy when he's fresh off hitting 27 home runs and leading the majors in RBI? If you're a contender, you keep Burleson. If you're a rebuilder like the Cardinals, you sell high now before free agency calls his name after the 2028 season.

Winn is more of a vexing case. He's elite defensively at shortstop, but he can't hit. If the Cardinals can get anything for him, they should take that W and the subsequent W of being able to move JJ Wetherholt back to shortstop.

Sure, Marte is coming off a down year that was marred by some bad optics . But he's also a three-time All-Star and sometimes-MVP contender, and he's on a club-friendly contract that runs through 2030. Because of that, he shouldn't be totally radioactive as a trade chip.

If Marte doesn't bring back the controllable starting pitching the D-backs reportedly seek, according to Nick Piecoro of The Arizona Republic , then they might have to offer up Jordan Lawlar, Ryan Waldschmidt or Tommy Troy to make it happen.

The Rockies need as much prospect depth as they can get, so Goodman absolutely needs to be back on the market this winter. He's slugged 72 home runs across the last two seasons, with good numbers away from Coors Field. He has three more years of club control left.

McCarthy and Castro are lesser gets as trade candidates, but each has his sweet spot. For Castro, it's defensive versatility. McCarthy can play all three outfield spots in his own right, and he's coming off his first 30-steal season.

The Dodgers need to get younger and more athletic on offense, and trading Hernández might accomplish that simply by addition through subtraction. He just shouldn't be expected to fetch much on his own, as he's a 34-year-old with a pricey contract who's coming off consecutive 1-WAR seasons.

If the Dodgers really want to make a splash, they'll open the door on all five of their top-100 prospects. That should include even Josue De Paula (No. 4), though maybe only if the return is on the Elly De La Cruz-level.

Trading Miller is a hard sell, but the idea was in the ether before the Padres took off and made the playoffs. They could get a huge haul for him if they actually did it, which could be especially useful for restocking a rotation that just lost Michael King to the free-agent market.

There isn't much to see among San Diego's other wares, though Fermin is worth a look as a backup catcher. He's currently sharing space with Ethan Salas and Luis Campusano, which isn't sustainable.

We say "bad" because Rafael Devers is a possible exception after a 37-homer season. Even so, he and Matt Chapman, Willy Adames and Jung Hoo Lee aren't really worth keeping anymore, so the Giants should open themselves back up to fielding interest in all four of them this winter.

Schmitt was a hot commodity on the summer trade market before he tore his meniscus in July. He should be again, as he can play just about anywhere and offers real power from the right side of the plate. Having three more seasons of club control doesn't hurt, either.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Ranking Rays SP Freddy Peralta's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: For most of Major League Baseball's 2026 campaign, dedicating an entire article to sorting out Freddy Peralta's market in free agency was an unlikely proposition.
articles.body:
For most of Major League Baseball's 2026 campaign, dedicating an entire article to sorting out Freddy Peralta's market in free agency was an unlikely proposition.

Peralta was an All-Star with the Brewers in both 2021 and 2025, entering 2026 with a 3.30 ERA over the previous half-decade. The Mets gave up two highly touted prospects (Jett Williams and Brandon Sproat) to acquire his final $8M season before hitting free agency for the first time.

They sure did regret it, though. In 22 starts with New York, Peralta had a 4.99 ERA. So, they sent him to Tampa Bay at the trade deadline for a trio of much less promising prospects than what they parted with to get him in January.

He turned things around almost immediately.

Including the postseason, Tampa Bay went 11-3 in his 14 starts. And after a couple of duds in August, he allowed just 10 earned runs over his last 55.1 innings pitched, good for an ERA of 1.63.

Maybe Fastball Freddy just loves pitching for small-market teams?

Unfortunately, it's looking like he'd be selling himself short to stay in that comfort zone.

Spotrac projects Peralta's market value at seven years, $201M, which is an absurd jump from when they had him projected at four years and $80M less than three weeks ago . Most likely, the actual answer is somewhere in the middle, close to the five-year, $130M deal Ranger Suarez signed this past winter.

Which teams have both the funds and the need for starting pitching to make that happen?

Boston Red Sox : Even if Sonny Gray doesn't return in 2027, Boston arguably doesn't need to add any pitching. Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett will all be back, with Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo also in the mix. Whatever spending the Red Sox are doing this winter, it ought to be on the lineup.

Houston Astros : This starting rotation is in rough shape, but so is Houston's projected payroll situation. Pending the arbitration salaries of Hunter Brown and Jeremy Peña, the Astros could be looking at north of $200M just for their top 10 earners. They would almost have to trade away one big salary in order to justify signing Peralta.

Los Angeles Dodgers : They don't need starting pitching. But if they decide they would like to add to their rotation, recent history sure does lead one to assume they would go all-in for Tarik Skubal instead of settling for Peralta.

New York Mets : They absolutely need pitching. They also absolutely have the funds. But if their plan for replacing guys like Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea who struggled for them in 2026 is to give nine figures to a guy who also struggled for them in 2026, that entire fan base would justifiably have a conniption.

New York Yankees : With Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón each signed through at least 2028, it's very unlikely the Yankees—who are already a projected $100M above the 2027 luxury tax threshold—would invest heavily in another starting pitcher. Though, as they seek their first World Series title since 2009, their desperation level has to be higher than usual.

Philadelphia Phillies : See: Yankees, New York. The Phillies already have a gargantuan payroll for next season, as well as one of the better starting rotations—especially if Andrew Painter's late-season arrival was for real. But they haven't won it all since 2008 and their window of opportunity to change that is rapidly closing.

Viable Candidates, But Not the Favorites

Atlanta Braves : Beyond Chris Sale, there are a lot of question marks in this rotation, many of which are of the "How many starts will (insert pitcher) be healthy enough to make?" variety. But spending big in free agency has never been the Atlanta way. Rather than signing Peralta, it's more likely they re-sign Tyler Mahle to a short-term deal and/or trade for one year of someone like Logan Gilbert.

Baltimore Orioles : For several consecutive offseasons, we've allowed ourselves to believe that it might be the year that Baltimore is going to really invest in its pitching staff. Instead, the O's keep taking half-measures, like trading for one year of Corbin Burnes or signing Charlie Morton, Kyle Gibson and Chris Bassitt to one-year deals. But, hey, maybe this actually is the year?

Miami Marlins : It's probably overly wishful thinking for a team that has invested a combined $28.5M in free agency over the past three winters, but a starting rotation of Peralta, Sandy Alcantara, Eury Pérez and Max Meyer would be a certified problem. And regardless of how things pan out with these CBA negotiations, the Marlins are going to be either strongly encouraged or actually required to do some spending for a change.

Minnesota Twins : The Twins are in a spot similar to where the Tigers were a year ago, staring down quite the long list of key players who will be free agents next winter. But instead of trading away Tarik Skubal and others, Detroit doubled down by signing Framber Valdez. Could the Twins go a similar route, bringing in Peralta on a multi-year deal now in preparation for the forthcoming departures of Joe Ryan and Pablo López?

San Diego Padres : The Padres definitely need some pitching, but Peralta is presumably their Plan B if Michael King opts out of the two years left on his contract and signs elsewhere. With Manny Machado's cash salary ballooning from $21M to $40M, they probably don't have room in the budget to sign two front-line starters. So, if King remains in San Diego, it'd be a bit shocking if they also land Peralta.

Texas Rangers : The Rangers were very intentional about trimming payroll this past winter, but they should be in the market for a multi-year starting pitcher, with Nathan Eovaldi and MacKenzie Gore both slated for free agency next offseason. (And with Jacob deGrom not getting any younger.) But upgrading the lineup figures to be their bigger focal point.

Washington Nationals : While it's a near-certainty that Washington will do some spending on pitching this winter, it has been almost seven years since they last invested more than $15M in a single free agent, averaging less than $25M spent in free agency over the past six offseasons. Trying to buy low on someone like Casey Mize or Patrick Sandoval is probably the direction they're more likely to go.

Milwaukee Brewers or Tampa Bay Rays : We know Peralta pitches well there, that he would be welcomed back with open arms and that each team could use another starting pitcher this winter. But Milwaukee has never spent more than $50M on a free agent pitcher, and Tampa Bay has never invested more than $40M into any free agent.

That said, if Peralta's market isn't anywhere near what we think it is and he ends up needing to settle for something more in the "one-year, $20M with a player option for a second season" type of range, maybe these teams become the co-favorites to re-sign him.

Current Options for 2026-27 Starting Rotation : Sean Burke, Hagen Smith, Davis Martin, Luis Castillo, Anthony Kay, Noah Schultz, Grant Taylor, Shane Smith

In case you weren't already aware heading into the playoffs, it became clear during Chicago's seven-game postseason run that this starting rotation wasn't exactly World Series-caliber.

Hagen Smith started more postseason games (three) than he had previously started in his major league regular-season career (one). And after almost leading the White Sox in innings pitched during the regular season, Anthony Kay lasted just three batters in his lone start of the postseason.

Sean Burke had some solid outings, but White Sox starters averaged just 7.6 outs in the postseason, repeatedly leaving the bullpen to do the heavy lifting.

To be sure, we have high hopes for Hagen Smith in 2027. The No. 5 overall pick in the 2024 draft played an unexpectedly huge role in the postseason less than two months after making his MLB debut, but he could be the ace of this staff if he gets his walks under control. (He walked eight of the 21 batters he faced in the ALDS and averaged 5.8 BB/9 between Triple-A and the majors during the regular season.)

The White Sox might need Peralta more than any other team does.

Here's the rub: Chicago has never spent more than $75M on a single contract (free agent or extension) and has only once spent more than $20M on a free agent starting pitcher, when it gave Dallas Keuchel a three-year, $55.5M deal in December 2019.

That doesn't mean it can't happen, of course. There's a first time for everything, and there ought to be an urgency to win in 2027 now that their time with Munetaka Murakami might already be halfway finished.

But we'll believe they're willing to give someone a nine-figure contract once they actually do it.

Current Options for 2026-27 Starting Rotation : Framber Valdez, Keider Montero, Troy Melton, Jackson Jobe, River Ryan, Drew Anderson, Reese Olson, Andrew Sears

This season was a bust for the Tigers, but they are set up for success in 2027.

The lineup, at any rate, could be great. The late-season arrivals of Max Clark and Hao-Yu Lee provided a lot of promise, and there's a non-zero chance Zyhir Hope—the main attraction going Detroit's way in the Tarik Skubal trade—will be starting in right field on Opening Day. The Tigers already had the American League's highest-scoring offense from June 1 through the end of the regular season, too.

Is this starting rotation potent/experienced enough, though?

With any luck, Valdez will be better in his second season with the Tigers, but Montero as the possible No. 2 arm with a career ERA of 4.08 isn't particularly reassuring. Yet, he has more MLB experience (344.0 IP) than Melton, Jobe and Ryan combined (283.2 IP).

Such is life when you lose all of Skubal, Casey Mize, Jack Flaherty and Justin Verlander from your previous Opening Day rotation.

Adding Freddy Peralta to serve as co-ace to Valdez could be the answer.

Detroit ended 2026 with an estimated tax payroll of $234M, but they are nowhere close to that threshold for next year with only two players (Valdez and Javier Báez) slated for serious earnings. They could sign Peralta and still end up well below their 2026 Opening Day payroll.

Current Options for 2026-27 Starting Rotation : Dylan Cease, Trey Yesavage, José Soriano, Cody Ponce, Spencer Miles, Spencer Arrighetti, Ricky Tiedemann, Jake Bloss

Toronto has a sensational ace in Cease, a respectable tandem behind him in Yesavage and Soriano and some substantial question marks from there.

As is, Ponce is almost certainly penciled in as the No. 4 starter, as the Blue Jays gave him a three-year, $30M deal last winter. However, he has logged a grand total of 2.1 innings pitched in the majors over the past five years, spending 2022-25 in Asia before injuring his ACL in his 2026 season debut. (He is expected to be fully recovered by Opening Day, if he isn't already.)

Arrighetti is their most experienced option for the other opening. Though, with a career ERA of 4.79 and FIP of 4.82, it hasn't exactly been encouraging experience.

Miles had a strong rookie season as a bulk reliever / spot starter and is perhaps the early front-runner for the No. 5 spot in this rotation. But he came out of nowhere, not advancing beyond Single-A ball until the Blue Jays plucked him from San Francisco in the Rule 5 Draft this past December. We shall see what he can do for an encore.

Or perhaps it's finally time for Tiedemann to shine? The once highly touted prospect underwent Tommy John surgery in July 2024 and didn't return to action until this past June. He did fare well, though, making his MLB debut this season. However, he didn't record more than five outs in any of his appearances at any level in 2026 and might just be a reliever moving forward.

Long story short, Toronto could really use at least one more sure thing in this rotation.

And while they do already have a substantial payroll for 2027, it's nothing compared to what it was on Opening Day 2026, now that George Springer ($25M), Kevin Gausman ($22M), Shane Bieber ($16M), Jeff Hoffman ($11M) and Daulton Varsho ($10.75M) are out of the picture.

There's plenty of room for a Peralta-sized contract, provided they have a similar budget. It's really just a question of whether they prioritize upgrading the rotation after ranking dead last in the majors in scoring in 2026.

Current Options for 2026-27 Starting Rotation : Logan Webb, Landen Roupp, Adrian Houser, Anthony Molina, Matt Wilkinson, Yunior Marté, César Perdomo

After trading away Robbie Ray and Tyler Mahle and losing both Adrian Houser and Trevor McDonald to the IL, San Francisco basically spent the final two months of the regular season holding open tryouts for its 2027 starting rotation.

Both Carson Whisenhunt and Blade Tidwell suffered UCL tears, joining McDonald and Hayden Birdsong on the list of Giants who will be recovering from Tommy John surgery in 2027. Between Molina, Wilkinson, Marté and Perdomo, only Molina gave them anything worth getting optimistic about with a 2.62 FIP in 29 innings of work.

And while both Roupp and Houser appear to be locked into starting gigs, it probably wouldn't be difficult to put together a ranking of the top 100 starting pitchers heading into 2027 without even considering either one.

In other words, this rotation could use a lot of help, particularly in the form of a front-line starter to pair with Webb.

The big question is whether they have the money to make it happen, considering they already owe Webb ($23M), Jung Hoo Lee ($22M), Rafael Devers ($23.5M), Matt Chapman ($25M) and Willy Adames ($28M) a combined $121.5M in 2027.

One more somewhat substantial salary should be doable, though, as they don't have much else to worry about. Houser is due $9.5M, but beyond him and those six contracts, there's little else in the way of substantial salary commitments.

Current Options for 2026-27 Starting Rotation : Justin Steele, Edward Cabrera, Ben Brown, Colin Rea, Javier Assad, Braxton Garrett, Jordan Wicks, Cade Horton (probably after All-Star Break)

It is no secret that the Chicago Cubs have a lot of work to do on their starting rotation.

Nine pitchers made at least nine starts for the Cubs this season, and they're going to need to replace at least six of them, possibly seven if they decline their $7.5M club option on Rea. And it was already one of the least valuable starting rotations in baseball aside from the Rockies and Athletics.

It's really just a question of which free agent starting pitcher (or pitchers) the Cubs decide to pursue most aggressively.

And if former Milwaukee Brewers manager Craig Counsell has any say in the matter, one would assume he'll be pushing hard for them to sign Peralta.

During the latter three of their six seasons together in Milwaukee, Peralta made 74 starts with a 3.41 ERA. Corbin Burnes and Brandon Woodruff were the brighter stars back then, but Peralta was a massive piece of the puzzle as Counsell oversaw the Brewers becoming the annual contender they are today.

It's not just Counsell in this organization who knows all too well what Peralta brings to the table. In his career, he has logged more innings pitched against the Cubs than any other team. And since the beginning of 2021, he has a 2.86 ERA in his 18 regular season starts against them.

If he can pitch like that for them instead of against them, the Cubs could be mighty dangerous.

articles.title: Top 2026 MLB Free Agents Rumors and Predictions on Landing Spots
articles.summary: The 2026 iteration of MLB free agency is here, and it could move with an urgency unseen in most offseasons.
articles.body:
The 2026 iteration of MLB free agency is here, and it could move with an urgency unseen in most offseasons.

That doesn't mean it will, obviously, but players and front offices may have incentive to get their deals done early with the collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1.

The market hasn't moved much yet in terms of finalized transactions, but talks are clearly happening. Let's dig into what the latest baseball buzz is all about and use it to help form predictions around the players involved.

After back-to-back losses in the ALDS, the New York Yankees could be busy trying to get their roster into World Series-contending shape. While it's too early to say what kind of additions they can make, it does seem like a few subtractions are already surfacing.

As ESPN's Jorge Castillo put it, "Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham are as good as gone."

This stops well short of qualifying as a jaw-dropping surprise, but it does represent a fairly big pivot. Both Chisholm and Grisham were top-eight on the team in at-bats during both the regular season and the playoffs. Splitting from them would mean needing to find new starters at both second base and center field.

Maybe the Yankees will trot out internal replacements, but if they're aiming for improvements, it wouldn't be at all surprising to see them target at least one external addition. As for Chisholm and Grisham, both have rich enough track records to anticipate soft landings in free agency.

Prediction: Chisholm signs with the Detroit Tigers, and Grisham joins the Cincinnati Reds.

Cubs Dreaming Big Ahead of Tarik Skubal Sweepstakes?

Save for the unknowns of the labor negotiations, free agency couldn't have timed out much better for Tarik Skubal. He is clearly the cream of this year's crop, and his ability to navigate around midseason elbow surgery and still deliver elite results suggests teams should be comfortable and confident in projecting similarly elite production moving forward.

He is, in short, the one obvious name-your-price free agent in this class. And because that price could be record-setting, his market figures to be limited to only the biggest spenders in baseball. That might mean this is headed toward a Los Angeles Dodgers-New York Mets staredown, but there are some other hopefuls wishing that won't be the case.

Per ESPN's Jeff Passan , the Chicago Cubs "badly want Skubal." Passan also mentioned the San Diego Padres as possible suitors, given their "need [for] a rotation anchor."

That being said, Passan also mentioned skepticism from the Cubs "that they will be willing to compete at the sort of dollars Skubal is expected to get." And Passan noted the Padres have coveted free agent pitchers of their own in Michael King and Nick Pivetta. So, this very well might be a Dodgers vs. Mets showdown in the end.

Prediction: Skubal re-signs with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Any fans unfamiliar with the name Teruaki Sato should plan on getting familiar with it pretty quickly. He is, at least according to The Athletic's Keith Law , the best position player on the market and the No. 2 free agent overall, trailing only Skubal.

Sato won the NPB's Triple Crown this past season, hitting .306 with 39 home runs and 106 RBI. The 27-year-old has experience at third base and in the outfield, but he could also be a candidate to man second base or first base if his glove doesn't play up.

The way Law sees it, Sato "should blow away" the salaries that Kazuma Okamoto and Munetaka Murakami inked last offseason. Law projects a four- or five-year deal for Sato with "at least $25 million" annually. For reference, Okamoto got four years and $60 million from the Toronto Blue Jays, and Murakami cost the Chicago White Sox just $34 million over two seasons.

It certainly doesn't hurt Sato that both Okamoto (33 homers, 92 RBI) and Murakami (35 homers) fared well in their debut MLB campaigns. It probably helps even more that this free agent class looks light on difference-making bats, as suitors could share Law's opinion that Sato is the best on the board.

Prediction: Sato signs with the Los Angeles Angels.

articles.title: Mariners Hire Jason Kanzler as Manager to Replace Dan Wilson for 2027 MLB Season
articles.summary: After being one of the most disappointing teams in MLB last season, the Seattle Mariners are turning to Jason Kanzler to get them back on track in 2027.
articles.body:
After being one of the most disappointing teams in MLB last season, the Seattle Mariners are turning to Jason Kanzler to get them back on track in 2027.

Seattle confirmed the hire after MLB.com's Daniel Kramer reported Tuesday the team was expected to bring Kanzler aboard.

This will be his first managerial job. He is coming from the Chicago Cubs, where he was director of player development. Seattle also interviewed former Astros manager Joe Espada during the finalist stage.

The Mariners were expected to be among the top teams in the American League after reaching the ALCS in 2025. They brought back virtually every key contributor from that group, including all five primary starting pitchers.

Things never came together for a multitude of reasons. The rotation wasn't as good as expected. Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez had the worst offensive seasons of their careers.

On top of all of those struggles for the players, manager Dan Wilson frequently seemed lost with some of his in-game decisions. The result was a 76-86 record that led to Wilson being fired after just his second full season on the job.

It didn't help Wilson's case that the Mariners were largely non-competitive in an AL West that the Houston Astros won with 81 victories.

The failures from 2026 did show how high the expectations have gotten for the Mariners after their terrific 2025 in which they won the division and reached the ALCS for the first time in 24 years.

Kanzler is walking into a situation where there will be pressure on him to get the Mariners back on track, but the roster is set up for the Mariners to be good right away with better luck.

Kanzler isn't bringing any dugout experience with him to Seattle, but his track record as a coach is strong. He was hired to work in the Astros' minor-league system in 2019, worked his way up to the MLB staff in 2022 and finished as their hitting coach in 2023.

Following the 2023 season, Kanzler was hired by the Cubs to lead their player development.

Seattle hiring a manager with expertise in player development probably isn't a coincidence considering Colt Emerson, Kade Anderson, Lazaro Montes, and Michael Arroyo were all promoted to the big leagues last season.

That group, along with other prospects on the cusp of the big leagues like Ryan Sloan and Felnin Celesten, will be counted on to form the next great core for the Mariners.

Kanzler is walking into a good situation with a talented roster already in place. He just has to make all the pieces fit so the Mariners can get back to being a top-tier AL team like they were in 2025.

articles.title: MLB Reportedly Proposes Delaying Salary Cap Until 2028, Latest Details Revealed amid CBA Talks
articles.summary: A firm salary cap wouldn't go into effect until 2028 in the newest proposed collective bargaining agreement from MLB.
articles.body:
A firm salary cap wouldn't go into effect until 2028 in the newest proposed collective bargaining agreement from MLB.

The league said Tuesday it would set the cap at $258.2 million and the floor at $180.2 million.

ESPN's Jeff Passan noted those figures are slight increases from MLB's last proposal:

The MLBPA said in a rebuttal on Tuesday that the proposal to delay the cap until 2028 would still bring "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights."

The salary floor would trigger massive investment across the sport. Half of the 30 teams spent less than $180.2 million on payroll in 2026, per Spotrac , and hitting that number would require more than doubling their spending in the cases of the Miami Marlins and Cleveland Guardians.

Of course, a hard cap would hit MLB's biggest spenders significantly. The New York Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees were north of $300 million.

The effects of inflation also mean that $258.2 million in 2028 doesn't equal the same as it does now.

From the ownership side, pushing the salary cap back another year would give front offices more time to plan and clean up the books as necessary. That could make it easier to build a consensus.

Players are unlikely to be moved, however, when they've long pushed back against a salary cap in any form.

MLB Players Association interim executive director Bruce Meyer posited in June the effects of a cap would be sizable on future earnings.

"Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," he said, per The Athletic's Evan Drellich . "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

"Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."

The current CBA will expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1.

articles.title: MLB proposes delaying salary cap and floor until 2028 season so free agency can proceed before lockout
articles.summary: The league is trying to encourage free-agent deals to get done before Dec. 1.
articles.body:
With a lockout looming on Dec. 1, MLB doesn't want free agency at a complete standstill until then. Because of that, the league has altered one of its biggest demands ahead of collective bargaining agreement (CBA) negotiations with the players' union.

To incentivize free-agent signings ahead of the lockout and smooth the transition to a new economic system, MLB has proposed the implementation of a salary cap and salary floor ahead of the 2028 season, rather than beginning in 2027. That could make it easier for teams to negotiate and sign free agents in November, before a new CBA is put in place.

Additionally, MLB tweaked its proposed figures for a salary cap and floor. Under the new proposal, the league would set the salary cap at $258.2 million. The salary floor would be $180.2 million. Those figures are up from MLB's previous proposal, which called for a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor .

But the implementation of a salary cap and floor has not been agreed upon by the league and MLBPA. It, in fact, remains one of the most contentious issues surrounding the upcoming CBA negotiations and a nonstarter for the players' union.

While owners have pushed for a cap for many years, the league has made it the most pressing issue on the table ahead of this latest round of CBA negotiations. But the players' union has expressed vehement opposition to a salary cap for decades — and reiterated that stance on Tuesday.

MLB went as far as building an entire campaign around the idea that a salary cap and floor are necessary to "fix" the game. That campaign launched in June. Four months later, the Milwaukee Brewers, the team with the 19th-highest payroll in baseball , defeated the Tampa Bay Rays, the team with the 25th-highest payroll in baseball, in the World Series.

In its campaign, MLB focused its ire on the Los Angeles Dodgers. While the team did reach the National League Championship Series, it was the only team with an above-average payroll to reach that stage of the playoffs this year. The fourth team to play in the Championship Series was the Cleveland Guardians, who had the 30th-highest payroll last season.

Despite that outcome, MLB still intends to push for a salary cap and floor in CBA negotiations. Tuesday's proposal shows the league might be somewhat flexible with the implementation of a cap and floor, though it's unclear how much this change will stimulate the free-agent market.

And even in a scenario in which the union would be open to the idea, pushing the implementation of a cap and floor back one season doesn't truly help teams and players sign deals now. While Tuesday's proposal would allow teams to operate as normal in 2027, it still presents a ton of uncertainty for 2028 and beyond. That's a major problem for any teams or players looking to negotiate multiyear contracts.

And again, this proposal focuses on the timing of something that has not been agreed upon by the league and the players' union. A salary cap and floor are far from a certainty and might not be implemented at all.

articles.title: What does the latest labor proposal from MLB actually mean?
articles.summary: The league has adjusted how and when it wants to add a salary cap, but the issue remains a nonstarter for the players' union.
articles.body:
In the first major labor development of the offseason, MLB on Tuesday proposed postponing the implementation of a salary cap until the 2028 season. The goal of such a delay, according to a league social media post , would be to "allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits."

Also notable is a change made by the league to the proposed cap and floor figures, with the potential cap rising from $245.3 million to $258.2 million and the floor moving from $171.2 million to $180.2 million.

With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1 , the entire baseball industry is bracing for an extended work stoppage. This most recent proposal from the league won't do a thing to stop that oncoming storm, with the MLB Players Association vehemently opposed to even the mention of a capped system, a stance they reiterated later Tuesday . Yet owners and league officials have continued pushing passionately for a cap, citing a perceived lack of competitive balance and fan frustration toward big-market spenders such as the Los Angeles Dodgers.

So does Tuesday's news mean anything? Not really, considering how much the cap remains a nonstarter for the union.

Above all else, this latest proposal is a sign that the league is attempting to shift conversations about the cap from the theoretical to the actual. MLB's openness to delaying the cap is a recognition of the inevitable logistical conundrum that rolling out a new system would cause.

In the difficult-to-envision world in which the union relents and agrees to a cap and floor this winter, there'd likely be an extremely truncated window between CBA ratification and Opening Day. Front offices would thus need to quickly familiarize themselves with a new system and operate under said system to complete the offseason, all while getting under a cap or above a floor. That's an unrealistic path forward.

MLB's latest proposal would simplify that process, giving teams more time to adjust to a new economic system. It also might precipitate more transactional offseason activity before the work stoppage (and the corresponding dead period) begins. Teams, in theory, would be more willing to commit dollars and trade players if they know what they're looking at for 2027 and will have a grace period to adjust to the cap. Whether that actually happens, though, is anybody's guess.

"The projected cap and floor payrolls for 2028 would make 12 clubs increase payroll by $636M to reach the floor, and 8 clubs to decrease payroll $528M to reach the cap," the league's statement said .

"Coming off another incredible season of baseball, MLB owners continue to propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values," the union said in its response .

The league might view their revised cap and floor figures as a bargaining concession, a good faith ceding of ground, but the union most certainly does not. The MLBPA has steadfastly opposed a salary cap throughout its entire existence and has shown no signs of relenting during the current round of negotiations.

That's one thing that did not change on Tuesday.

articles.title: Pat Murphy Addresses Viral Video Ripping 'Horses--t' Yankees After Brewers' World Series Win
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy went viral after his team clinched a World Series title in Game 5 for telling first baseman and pending free agent Jake Bauers that he was going to be a "a rich f--ker" and to "just remember when you are on that horses--t [New York] Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourselves? Just remember, say, 'This is the way we used to do it.'"
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy went viral after his team clinched a World Series title in Game 5 for telling first baseman and pending free agent Jake Bauers that he was going to be a "a rich f--ker" and to "just remember when you are on that horses--t [New York] Yankees team and you guys are all playing for yourselves? Just remember, say, 'This is the way we used to do it.'"

But Murphy, who didn't realize he was on a "hot mic," said he called Yankees general manager Brian Cashman to clarify his remarks.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard [my comments] got out," he said during an appearance on the New York Post's "The Show" podcast (h/t ESPN ). "I tried to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees. I was just referring to the teams with a lot of money that sign a lot of players that sometimes end up not being that 'Little Engine that Could,' so to speak—more of a high expectation, 'I gotta get mine.' I regret saying it."

"I felt horribly if I slandered the Yankees, because I was just kind of referring to them as this iconic machine," he added. "... It wasn't smart on my part, and I'm sorry about it."

Murphy said part of his comments were mirroring how he would joke with Bauers throughout the Brewers' run to a title.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand and I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,'" he said. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us, and you're going to forget all about how we did things. ... I would just give him this rhetoric every time."

The 31-year-old Bauers, who played for the Yankees in 2023, had a breakout 2026 campaign, setting career highs in homers (26), RBI (86), runs (93), batting average (.266) and OPS (.874). He also caught the final out of the World Series and gifted that ball to Murphy, which was when the manager made his Yankee comments.

While Murphy apologized for those remarks, there have indeed been legitimate questions about the leadership and clubhouse culture of the 2026 Yankees, including from prominent former players of the team like Hall of Famer CC Sabathia. That Murphy, albeit unintentionally, brought further attention to that storyline was hardly ideal for the Yankees.

articles.title: Brewers manager Pat Murphy says he called Yankees GM Brian Cashman to 'explain' profane comment after World Series

Bauers laughed off the comment, saying "You ain't getting rid of me that easy," but Yankees fans were less amused.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out … I heard the next morning, we're at the parade and everybody was talking about it. I was like, 'What? How did they hear that?'
