articles.title: Albert Pujols to Interview for Astros' Manager Job, Latest MLB Rumors on Search
articles.summary: The Houston Astros will interview Albert Pujols as part of their managerial search, according to The Athletic's Chandler Rome.
articles.body:
The Houston Astros will interview Albert Pujols as part of their managerial search, according to The Athletic's Chandler Rome .

The New York Post 's Jon Heyman provided more detail during a Bleacher Report stream:

Pujols is one of the greatest hitters of his generation. He was an 11-time All-Star and three-time National League MVP.

The 46-year-old managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic earlier this year. The country reached the semifinals and earned a bronze medal.

Pujols generated interest during the 2025-26 hiring cycle, and he advanced deep into the process with the San Diego Padres before they opted for Craig Stammen.

Rome noted Pujols already has a connection to the Astros' recently hired general manager Randy Flores. They were teammates for five seasons in St. Louis.

Daikin Park is familiar territory for the retired slugger as well. He played more games against the Astros than any other team, having twice shared a division with them.

Houston ultimately advanced, but Pujols dealt closer Brad Lidge a psychic blow with his home run in Game 5 of the 2005 NLCS.

There would be some irony in him sitting in the Astros dugout after being a thorn in the franchise's side for so long.

Former catcher Brad Ausmus is reportedly on their radar in the manager search, and Rome reported Texas Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta will interview.

Ausmus and Urueta have far more coaching experience than Pujols, which could give them an edge. Ausmus in particular "will be buoyed by his longtime friendship with Jeff Bagwell" in the words of Rome.

A lot of fans would probably welcome the hiring of somebody from outside Bagwell's orbit, and Pujols fits that label. The fact he's largely unproven as a manager would present some risk, though.

articles.title: Cleveland Guardians Pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz Described as 'Cheaters' at Trial
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz were described by a prosecutor Wednesday as "cheaters" during opening statements at a New York criminal fraud trial that has cast a spotlight on the threat gamblers pose to America's pastime.
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz were described by a prosecutor Wednesday as "cheaters" during opening statements at a New York criminal fraud trial that has cast a spotlight on the threat gamblers pose to America's pastime.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Urquiola told a jury in Brooklyn that Clase befriended a sports betting gambler in the Dominican Republic in early 2023 who shared his interest in dominoes and cockfighting, which is legal in his home country.

Clase eventually agreed to tell "his new friend" what kinds of pitches he would throw in certain games, enabling gamblers to reap at least $460,000 on platforms that allow customers to bet on whether a pitch would be a ball or a strike, she said.

"The defendants, Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, are cheaters," Urquiola told jurors. She said they "sold their pitches."

Clase, the Guardians' former star closer, and Ortiz, a starter, have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on non-disciplinary leave from the club without pay while facing prosecution. They were arrested in November 2025 and have been free on bail since.

Prosecutors said Clase began providing information about his pitches to bettors in 2023 and recruited Ortiz into the scheme in 2025.

Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time American League Reliever of the Year who had completed the fourth season of a $20 million, five-year contract when conspiracy and fraud charges against the pitchers were made public in November 2025.

Ortiz, 27, earned $782,600 as a starting pitcher for the Guardians during the 2025 season.

Urquiola said Clase saw gamblers profiting from his pitches and "decided it wasn't enough to help his friends make money," so he asked for kickbacks.

She said text messages in which the pitchers described rigged pitches and bets, sometimes using code words such as "chicken" or "rooster," along with testimony from some gamblers, would prove the government's case.

Defense lawyers, however, said their clients were innocent and that a gambler who befriended Clase falsely claimed to other gamblers that the pitcher was providing inside information on his pitches and tried to sell them the information.

Michael Bronson, an attorney for Clase, said his client attended school until age 15 in a small coastal village in the Dominican Republic before focusing on baseball and becoming "a standout, a superstar" with a reputation for shutting down teams in the final inning of games.

He said Clase was 25 in the spring of 2023 when he met a 41-year-old gambler, Enoc Pena, who made over 7,000 bets from 2023 to 2025 and had a history of lying to get what he wanted.

Pena "didn't see a peer, a friend. He saw a mark," Bronson said.

Soon Pena was bringing Clase food and picking him up at the airport in the Dominican Republic, the lawyer said. The pitcher, in turn, gave him tickets to Guardians games and loaned him money.

As Pena bragged to fellow gamblers that he was close to Clase and tried to sell them information, he was actually guessing which pitches Clase would throw in games and managed with fellow gamblers to lose over 200 bets on Clase's pitches, the lawyer said.

Pena was "selling lies," Bronson said, urging jurors to ask themselves if his client would risk "a fortune and his lifelong dream over a few thousand dollars."

Attorney Samuel Landes, representing Ortiz, told jurors in an opening statement that the pitcher had no contact with gamblers and that only two of his pitches, both balls, are at stake in the trial.

"That's not a conspiracy. That's just baseball," he said.

At one point, Landes asked his client to stand as he introduced him to the jury. Ortiz stood up and waved.

Landes said Ortiz was victimized by Pena's lies, including allegations that the pitcher — who had received $1.7 million in advance for future contracts and stood to make millions more — had accepted $5,000 for tips about his pitches.

"Why would Luis Ortiz throw all that away for $5,000? He would not," he said.

Landes said Pena had struck a deal with prosecutors allowing him to avoid prison and stay in the U.S. despite lying to banks and about his marital status on immigration forms.

Although Pena was once listed as a possible witness at the trial, prosecutors said last week that they did not intend to put him on the witness stand.

articles.title: Albert Pujols to reportedly interview for Astros' managerial opening
articles.summary: Albert Pujols continues to receive interest as an MLB manager.
articles.body:
One of the greatest MLB players of the previous era will interview for another open managerial job. St. Louis Cardinals legend Albert Pujols will reportedly meet with the Houston Astros to discuss the team's managerial vacancy , according to The Athletic.

It's not the first time Pujols has interviewed to be an MLB manager. He interviewed for the Los Angeles Angels and San Diego Padres vacancies last season, though he was not chosen for either position.

The Padres opted to hire Craig Stammen. The Angels might have been interested in Pujols, but reports suggested the two sides couldn't agree on contract terms , resulting in the Angels turning to Kurt Suzuki, who accepted a one-year deal with the team. The Angels declined to bring Suzuki back for 2027 and are searching for a new manager again this offseason.

While Pujols has not managed in the major leagues, he does have experience as a skipper. Following his retirement from baseball after the 2022 season, Pujols was named manager of the Leones del Escogido in the Dominican Republic in 2024. He helped lead the team to victory in the Serie Final during the 2024-25 season and the 2025 Caribbean Series. Pujols also managed Team Dominican Republic to a third-place finish at the 2026 World Baseball Classic.

Pujols should have a friendly audience when he attends his interview, as he was teammates with new Astros general manager Randy Flores. The pair spent four seasons together with the Cardinals, including a World Series-winning season in 2006.

Flores was asked about the possibility of talking to former teammates about the Astros' managerial opening when he was introduced as the team's general manager. At the time, he declined to get into specifics, saying he would lean on "network, experience and expertise" when considering candidates. In addition to Pujols, the team is expected to speak with Luis Urueta, the Texas Rangers' bench coach, and Brad Ausmus, the New York Yankees' bench coach, per The Athletic.

The Astros are in the market for a new manager after parting ways with Joe Espada in October. Espada spent three seasons as the team's skipper, putting up a 256-229 record.

Despite his regular-season success, Espada went into the 2026 MLB season in the final year of his contract. The Astros signaled they weren't bringing the manager back in October, allowing him to interview for the Seattle Mariners' open managerial job despite Espada still technically being under contract in Houston. The Mariners opted to hire Jason Kanzler instead.

Whomever the Astros hire will likely face high expectations in Year 1. Although Houston won just 81 games in 2026, that was good enough to reach the postseason, where the Astros lost in the wild-card round to the Chicago White Sox. It was a disappointing result for the Astros, who have made the postseason in 10 of the past 12 seasons.

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors Reveal MLB Free Agency Plans Ahead of Potential Lockout
articles.summary: Jack Cury of Yes expects the New York Yankees, along with most MLB teams, to be active in free agency ahead of the likely Dec. 1 lockout and offered his take on which positions the team may look to improve upon.
articles.body:
Jack Cury of Yes expects the New York Yankees, along with most MLB teams, to be active in free agency ahead of the likely Dec. 1 lockout and offered his take on which positions the team may look to improve upon.

"When I look at the Yankees, I look at that bullpen as an area of need," he said during an appearance on The Michael Kay Show . "I look at third base as an area of need. I think they're looking at second and centerfield as well, figure out what they want to do in those spots. So yes, I do expect the Yankees to be active."

While the Yankees went 93-68 and reached the ALDS, getting swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in that series ultimately rendered the season a failure, at least according to most fans. There seems to be a real desire to see the Yankees fundamentally retool the lineup around Aaron Judge and improve the bullpen as well.

But perhaps the team could also view a major splash and enter the Tarik Skubal market.

As ESPN's Kiley McDaniel reported, "The Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets are the primary bidders, the Detroit Tigers are monitoring for a discount, the Yankees are thinking about it (and then trading from their pitching stockpile if they land Skubal), and the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and San Diego Padres are the sleepers with ownership changes behind the interest."

Skubal is probably a long shot. Adding him would limit the other moves the team could make, and plenty of moves are likely needed. But there isn't a safer—or more expensive—bet this winter than the perennial ace.

ESPN's David Schoenfield believes Japanese third baseman and outfielder Teruaki Sato would be a good potential fit and target for the Yankees, and he may be the top player on the market not named Skubal. We already know that Pat Murphy believes Jake Bauers will end up on the Yankees. And John Harper of SNY predicted the Yankees to end up with catcher Ryan Jeffers and second baseman Luis Arráez.

The theme here is that the Yankees could go in a lot of different directions as they seek to improve their roster. Expect them to be in the mix for a number of prominent free agents over the next month.

articles.title: Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz called 'cheaters' as gambling case opening statements begin in court
articles.summary: A federal attorney called Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz "cheaters" who "sold their pitches" as the Cleveland Guardians gambling case went to trial.
articles.body: Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz were in a Brooklyn court on Wednesday during opening statements in their gambling case. The relievers are accused of rigging their own pitches during games to benefit bettors. Both have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on non-disciplinary leave from the club without pay while facing prosecution. They were arrested in November 2025 and have been free on bail since. The pitchers were described by Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Urquiola Wednesday as "cheaters" during opening statements , and she said they "sold their pitches." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Urquiola said Clase befriended a sports betting gambler in the Dominican Republic in early 2023 who shared his interest in dominoes and cockfighting, which is legal in his home country. She said Clase saw gamblers profiting from his pitches and "decided it wasn't enough to help his friends make money," so he asked for kickbacks. Clase eventually agreed to tell "his new friend" what kinds of pitches he would throw in certain games, enabling gamblers to reap at least $460,000 on platforms that allow customers to bet on whether a pitch would be a ball or a strike, she said. Defense lawyers, however, said their clients were innocent and that a gambler who befriended Clase falsely claimed to other gamblers that the pitcher was providing inside information on his pitches and tried to sell them the information. He said Clase was 25 in the spring of 2023 when he met a 41-year-old gambler, Enoc Pena, who made over 7,000 bets from 2023 to 2025 and had a history of lying to get what he wanted. Pena "didn't see a peer, a friend. He saw a mark," Bronson said. WORLD SERIES CHAMPION MARK TEIXEIRA WINS US HOUSE SEAT IN TEXAS: 'I'M EXCITED' Soon Pena was bringing Clase food and picking him up at the airport in the Dominican Republic, the lawyer said. The pitcher, in turn, gave him tickets to Guardians games and loaned him money. As Pena bragged to fellow gamblers that he was close to Clase and tried to sell them information, he was actually guessing which pitches Clase would throw in games and managed with fellow gamblers to lose over 200 bets on Clase's pitches, the lawyer said. Pena was "selling lies," Bronson said, urging jurors to ask themselves if his client would risk "a fortune and his lifelong dream over a few thousand dollars." Bettors allegedly won $400,000 from betting platforms on pitches thrown by Clase between 2023 and 2025. Ortiz allegedly joined the scheme in June 2025. In one instance, the indictment alleges, Clase used his phone in the middle of a game to coordinate with a bettor on a pitch he would throw. Clase turned himself into arguably the game's best closer, pitching to a 1.21 ERA in his last full season in 2024, which was good for a third-place finish in the American League Cy Young Award vote. His 2025 ERA was 3.80 by the time he was investigated. Ortiz boasts a lifetime 4.36 ERA, with his best season also coming in 2024 with a 3.32 ERA. Clase inked a five-year, $20 million deal just before opening day in 2022, a few months after finishing fifth in the AL Rookie of the Year voting. Ortiz was making the veteran minimum of $782,600 last season because he was not yet arbitration eligible. articles.title: Bryce Harper implies there won't be a 2027 MLB season, admits he enjoys offseason more than playing
articles.summary: Bryce Harper's TikTok comments hint that the 2027 Major League Baseball season could be canceled as a lockout over a salary cap looms large.
articles.body: Major League Baseball has started its free agency period, and unlike most similar times in years past, there's a sense of urgency. The long-awaited lockout is rapidly approaching, with the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement on December 1. Given the two competing statements released this week, one from the league office purposefully rejecting the reality of baseball, and the Players Association reaffirming their united front against a potential salary cap, that lockout is essentially a guarantee. With the only question still up for debate how long that lockout lasts. Some on the optimistic side believe that the two sides will find a way to come to an agreement before games are canceled. MLB finally has some momentum on its side, as ratings and attendance have continued to grow. Although the World Series pitting two small market teams against each other predictably did not do as well as 2024-2025 with the Dodgers, Yankees, and Blue Jays involved. YANKEES PRESIDENT RANDY LEVINE SAYS HE IS 'CONFIDENT' MLB WILL AVOID A LOCKOUT DESPITE CAP FIGHT But the general trend for baseball is positive. Both sides need that to continue, monetarily, making the incentives seemingly more aligned for compromise. Then there's the pessimistic side. The negative case is that owners have realized that many fans are totally unaware of how baseball works and have come down on the side of salary caps. Apparently convinced that the reward for owners who refuse to spend money should be enshrined rules to ensure that they never have to spend too much. While locking in a sizable increase in franchise valuations that does nothing to "fix" the nonexistent competitive balance "issues," but does make the league's owners significantly richer. ONE OF MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL'S OWNERS JUST DESTROYED THE LEAGUE'S ENTIRE ARGUMENT FOR A LOCKOUT That would, in theory, mean owners dig their heels in to make themselves richer, always a good bet, while players refuse to budge on a system that protects their ability to enter a free market. One of the pessimists, apparently? Philadelphia Phillies superstar Bryce Harper. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Harper took to the TikTok comment section this week and responded to a few posts in a way that, uh, raised some eyebrows about both his interest in playing and the future of the 2027 regular season. In response to one post saying, "It seems like March through October is the off-season," Harper said, "It will be this year," in a clear reference to canceling 2027. Then another commentator added, "He likes the offseason more than the season atp (at this point)." Harper posted in response, "This is true." Nobody has ever questioned Bryce Harper's commitment to playing hard and giving every available ounce of effort when he's on the field. He's played in nearly 2,000 games since his debut in 2012, played in all 162 games for the first time in his career in 2026 in his age-33 season, and is well on his way to being a first ballot Hall of Famer. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER But admitting you like the offseason more than the regular season isn't a great look. It just isn't. And it's going to give off an Anthony Rendon-ish impression, that baseball is an annoyance rather than a passion. And to be fair to Harper, the regular season in MLB is grueling. It's 162 games in around 185 days, involving constant travel, little rest, and long nights. There's also an extremely, maybe unnecessarily, long spring training. He's also added another 60 career postseason games. That said, he's paid extremely well to deal with those challenges, like, $330 million over 13-years well. It doesn't seem like too much to ask to have some enthusiasm for it. Even if feigned. Here's hoping Harper is wrong about the 2027 season though. Regardless of what the ultimate system turns out to be, all baseball fans, for or against a cap, should be united in wanting the sport to have a regular season. Jeopardizing the future wouldn't help anyone. Unless you really enjoy being at home.

articles.title: New CBA proposal adjusts salary cap, floor
articles.summary: More money is on the table
articles.body:
Major League Baseball has amended its salary cap and floor proposal to the MLB Players Association. Now that the 2026 season is complete and baseball is into its offseason, MLB has proposed delaying the start of the salary cap and floor to the 2028 season. The rest of their proposals would begin with the 2027 season but the teams would have a full season to make adjustments to prepare themselves for the coming changes.

The owners further proposed increasing the cap to $258.2 million from the original $245.3 million and the floor to $180.2 million from $171.2 million. The new numbers reflect a 50-50 split of the projected revenue for the 2028 season.

The offer also includes $282 million in luxury tax revenue to be given to players in cash payments instead of being placed into retirement benefits. In the present system, when a team pays luxury tax, half of the money goes into player benefits and the other half to the teams. For the 2027 season, the league is offering to pay the retirement portion directly to the players. According to league estimates , $285,000 would go to each player who received a full year of service time, $213,400 to a player with three-quarters of a year of service, $142,300 to a player with a half year of service, and $71,100 to any player with a quarter year of service.

Per the MLB numbers, 12 teams would have to raise payroll to meet the minimum proposed floor while eight teams would have to decrease their payroll to meet the cap. Those numbers are based on current payrolls and would change based on what teams spend in 2027.

The MLB Players Association predictably responded negatively to the new offer.

"MLB owners continue to propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The statement continued, "a massive reduction in player compensation, elimination of fundamental player rights, plus a gutting of domestic and international amateur entry systems." A statement virtually identical to the previous proposal from the owners.

This appears to be an attempt by the league to sweeten the deal for the players but doesn't seem to have the desired effect. The baseline for the union is their unwillingness to accept a salary cap and floor as the start of negotiations.

The current contract expires and 11:59 pm eastern time on Dec. 1. The owners have made it clear they intend to lock the players out if no deal is reached by that time.

articles.title: MLB Moneyball Rankings: Which Team Got the Most Value from 2026 Roster?
articles.summary: The wide range of advanced statistics available in today's game has changed the way talent is evaluated and teams are assembled across Major League Baseball.
articles.body:
The wide range of advanced statistics available in today's game has changed the way talent is evaluated and teams are assembled across Major League Baseball.

The origins of that shift in philosophy can be traced back to the Moneyball days in the Oakland Athletics organization during the early 2000s.

Whether it's a small-market club trying to squeeze the most out of every spot on the roster or a large-market team with a seemingly endless cash flow, every dollar has to be spent with a clear purpose.

It's all about getting the most value out of players, from pre-arbitration guys contributing at a young age to big-money stars living up to their lofty paychecks.

Which club got the most value out of its roster in 2026?

ARI | ATH | ATL | BAL | BOS | CHC | CIN | CLE | COL | CWS | DET | HOU | KC | LAA | LAD | MIA | MIL | MIN | NYM | NYY | PHI | PIT | SD | SEA | SF | STL | TB | TEX | TOR | WSH

There are a lot of numbers to digest here, so here's a quick explanation.

Total Net Value was the ultimate factor in determining where each team landed in the rankings and was calculated as follows:

Step 1: Find each player's WAR total for the 2026 season, courtesy of Baseball Reference .

Step 2: Based on the FanGraphs value metric , the market value of 1 WAR was once again right around $8 million. So each player's WAR from Step 1 was multiplied by eight to give us the player's 2026 value in millions of dollars.

Step 3: Each player's 2026 salary was then subtracted from his 2026 value, resulting in his 2026 net value. Player salaries came from the team pages of Spotrac .

Formula: (2026 WAR x 8) - 2026 salary = 2026 net value

After that, the cumulative net values of all players who were part of the MLB payroll at any point in 2026 were totaled to determine each team's total net value.

Included is a look at each team's five best and five worst values, along with a notable observation for each club's value breakdown.

For those of you looking for a complete picture of your favorite team, a link to a full breakdown in the form of a Google Sheets document can be found under the total net value for each club.

For a team that has tried and failed for years to throw money at free agents in hopes of buying a title, it's fitting that the three best values on the roster by a landslide were a trio of homegrown rookies. Will Carson Benge or Nolan McLean give Sal Stewart a run for his money in the NL Rookie of the Year race?

High-profile offseason additions Bo Bichette, Jorge Polanco, Marcus Semien, Devin Williams (-$20.0M), Luis Robert Jr. (-$9.9M) and Freddy Peralta (-$9.6M) contributed a combined $129.1 million in negative net value.

Still pre-arbitration and making less than $1 million in 2026, closer Louis Varland was one of baseball's most dominant bullpen arms, posting a 1.27 ERA and 11.2 K/9 with 35 saves in 71 appearances. The lack of star power on this list speaks volumes to why Toronto ultimately fell short of expectations.

1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.: -$21.3 million

In the first season of his massive 14-year, $500 million extension, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. hit .260/.332/.356 for a 90 OPS+ with just nine home runs in 609 plate appearances. Guerrero is still only 27 years old, so there's no reason to believe his power has simply dried up. His batted-ball metrics were also strong.

Young slugger Bryce Eldridge will not be arbitration-eligible for the first time until after the 2028 season, so he has a chance to dominate the best value spot for the foreseeable future. The 22-year-old had a 133 OPS+ and 17 home runs in 107 games.

If there's a glass-half-full takeaway for the Giants, it's the fact that Matt Chapman (-$3.4M) and Willy Adames (-$7.4M) managed to stay off the worst values list. They have a lot of money tied up in a few high-priced veterans, and they will need to earn their money to right the ship after a 97-loss season.

If not for the tremendous value that Cristopher Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo provided while earning a combined $20.05 million and racking up 14.6 WAR, the Phillies' net value would look far worse than the already lackluster number that landed them in the No. 27 spot on this list.

Shortstop Trea Turner has seven years and $190.9 million remaining on his contract, and he's coming off the worst season of his career with an 81 OPS+ and negative-0.1 WAR in 157 games. The Phillies have a lot of money tied up in aging veteran stars, and Turner is the face of that overarching issue.

TJ Rumfield, Brennan Bernardino, Jake McCarthy and Tomoyuki Sugano (+$9.3M) were all low-cost additions for the Rockies on the trade market and in free agency, and they played a significant role in getting Colorado out of the red. They were No. 30 in these rankings a year ago, with a negative $155.9 million net value.

Kris Bryant last took the field in an MLB game on April 12, 2025, as chronic lumbar degenerative disk disease threatens to be a career-ending issue. The 34-year-old has two years and $54 million remaining on his seven-year, $182 million deal, and so far he has played 170 total games over the life of that contract.

Peter Lambert spent the 2025 season pitching for the Yakult Swallows in the Japanese League and returned stateside last offseason in a move that generated few headlines. The 29-year-old ended up leading the Astros in innings pitched (155.2), strikeouts (154) and pitching WAR (3.1).

A 0.0 WAR season from Jose Altuve made him one of the worst values in all of baseball as he plays out a five-year, $125 million deal. The front-loaded contract will see his cash payroll hit drop from $30 million in 2027 to just $10 million in 2028 and 2029.

Elly De La Cruz, Chase Burns and Sal Stewart earned a combined $2.4 million in 2026, demonstrating the tremendous value of homegrown, star-caliber talent relative to high-priced veteran free agents. In his first year of arbitration, De La Cruz is projected to earn $7.9 million, which still would have netted $36.9 million in positive net value.

With Brady Singer reaching free agency and TJ Friedl designated for assignment in September, the Reds are out from under two of the worst values on their 2026 roster. On the flip side, third baseman Ke'Bryan Hayes is still owed $29 million over the next three years.

The Angels already traded one of their most valuable controllable assets when they flipped José Soriano to Toronto at the trade deadline, and they could aggressively shop Zach Neto and Reid Detmers this winter to continue jump-starting a long overdue rebuild.

Left-hander Yusei Kikuchi was an All-Star in 2025 when he logged a 3.99 ERA and 174 strikeouts in 178.1 innings, but shoulder issues limited him to 14 starts in 2026. The 35-year-old will earn $21.225 million in the final year of his contract in 2027, but he has the potential to recoup some of his lost value with a clean bill of health.

The Padres cast a wide net last offseason with minor league deals, and they struck gold with the Ty France signing. A 2022 All-Star during his time in Seattle, the veteran first baseman posted a 139 OPS+ with 24 doubles, 21 home runs and 72 RBI in a 4.5-WAR campaign.

Joe Musgrove and Yu Darvish both spent the entire 2026 season on the sidelines, which is part of the reason the Padres made what turned out to be a disastrous move to acquire Casey Mize from the Tigers at the deadline. Expensive veterans Manny Machado (-$9.0M) and Xander Bogaerts (-$7.4M) avoided the worst values list.

For an Athletics team that ranked 29th in the majors with a 5.61 ERA from the starting rotation, J.T. Ginn was one of the few bright spots. The 27-year-old had a 3.71 ERA, 1.24 WHIP and 121 strikeouts in 138.1 innings, carving out a rotation spot four years after he was acquired from the Mets for Chris Bassitt.

A quality starter the last several seasons, Jeffrey Springs was shelled to the tune of a 6.18 ERA in 142.2 innings. After serving up an .861 OPS and 35 home runs to opposing hitters, he had his $15 million club option declined and might need to settle for a minor league deal this winter.

Elite defensive metrics (16 DRS) helped Cole Young log a 4.4-WAR season, as he hit .246/.312/.381 with 19 doubles, 17 home runs and 66 RBI in a roughly league-average offensive season. Can the M's find a way to replace free agent Randy Arozarena's offensive production and overall value impact?

The Mariners offloaded Luis Castillo at the trade deadline, and Taylor Ward was just an unsuccessful two-month rental, so Seattle has a chance to make a solid climb up the rankings next year. Brendan Donovan (-$1.8M) and Cal Raleigh (-$3.0M) are also capable of a significant value rebound.

With a 2.13 ERA and 30 saves in 58 appearances, starter-turned-reliever Jacob Latz was one of the surprise breakout performers of the 2026 season. He earned an All-Star selection and anchored a bullpen that was expected to be a weakness, and with control through 2030, he is an extremely valuable player.

Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi produced a combined 2.9 WAR while earning $63 million in salary, putting them firmly atop the worst values list. As the Rangers look to get younger this offseason, one or both of those veteran starters could hit the trade block ahead of the final guaranteed year of their contracts.

With Aaron Judge, Gerrit Cole and other veteran stars missing time to injury, AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and 41-homer slugger Ben Rice stepped up in a big way for the Yankees in breakout seasons. The bullpen also got a major boost from Paul Blackburn (62 G, 1.69 ERA, 3.1 WAR) in his first season as a full-time reliever.

A $25 million salary in 2027, of which $10 million will be paid by the Marlins, and a $10 million buyout on a 2028 club option are the only remaining financial obligations for Giancarlo Stanton. The Yankees are also shedding the $22.025 million that Trent Grisham earned on a qualifying offer, so there is some salary relief on the horizon.

While the best values list is lacking in high-profile talent outside of shortstop Gunnar Henderson, it's worth mentioning that Trevor Rogers (+$11.4M), Pete Alonso (+$8.2M) and Shane Baz (+$6.2M) all made positive value contributions. That was an especially promising result from Alonso in the first season of his five-year, $155 million deal.

Signed to bridge the gap at the back of the bullpen while Félix Bautista continued recovering from shoulder surgery, Ryan Helsley made just 17 appearances and logged eight saves before he was sidelined with his own arm issues. The two-time All-Star exercised his $14 million player option for 2027.

Carter Jensen (120 OPS+, 27 HR, 3.3 WAR) and Jac Caglianone (132 OPS+, 23 HR, 3.2 WAR) both delivered on their top prospect pedigrees with breakout seasons, giving the Royals a much-needed offensive boost alongside superstar Bobby Witt Jr.

Two years after finishing runner-up in AL Cy Young voting, and in the first season of a new two-year, $46 million deal, Seth Lugo had the worst ERA (5.17) of any qualified starter. He turns 37 years old later this month, and will be counted on to bounce back in 2027.

Grant Holmes (29 GS, 3.44 ERA, 151.2 IP, 2.7 WAR) and Martín Pérez (26 GS, 3.04 ERA, 142.0 IP, 2.9 WAR) were both instrumental in propping up an Atlanta starting rotation that was beset by injuries. Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle (+$10.8M) and Bryce Elder (+$8.8M) also provided solid value for a starting staff that was a surprise strength.

Rough seasons from Austin Riley and Ronald Acuña Jr. (-$1.8M) took a major bite out of Atlanta's offensive firepower, and there could be significant changes coming this offseason after the club's disappointing showing in the NLDS. The Braves exercised Acuña's $17 million club option for 2027 and hold a matching option for 2028.

Gabriel Moreno became the fifth catcher in MLB history to win a batting title (.311 BA) while also winning his second career Gold Glove, and he did it while playing on a $2.55 million contract. The 26-year-old is controllable through 2028, but could be an extension candidate in the near future.

Even earning just $8 million in 2026 with a significant chunk of his salary deferred, Zac Gallen was still one of the worst values on the D-backs roster. The high-profile trio of Gallen, Corbin Burnes and Merrill Kelly earned a combined $47 million and produced negative-1.7 WAR.

The four top values on the Detroit roster, along with outfielders Riley Greene (+$15.8M) and Max Clark (+$9.4M), represent the core the Tigers will build around going forward after a year of transition. The eight-year, $150 million extension that Kevin McGonigle signed in April could be one of the best bargains in baseball for years to come.

The Tigers are entering the final year of Javier Báez's six-year, $140 million contract, and through the first five years of that deal, he has tallied just 3.4 WAR over 544 games. He will earn $24 million in 2027, and will be a candidate to be released if there is not a clear role for him on the Opening Day roster.

With 9.8 WAR in a 40/40 season that is expected to end in NL MVP honors, Pete Crow-Armstrong provided the most net value of any player in baseball, and his six-year, $115 million extension immediately looks like a stroke of genius by the Cubs' front office.

Veteran starter Jameson Taillon was released in the final season of his four-year, $68 million contract, so the worst value on the Cubs roster will no longer be on the books in 2027. The North Siders essentially need to rebuild their entire rotation, and how they spend that money will go a long way in determining where they fit in these rankings a year from now.

The Griffin Jax-for-Taj Bradley trade at the 2025 deadline proved to be a win-win deal in 2026, with Jax helping to pitch the Rays to the World Series, while Bradley emerged as a controllable frontline arm in Minnesota. Still only 25, he went 12-6 with a 3.73 ERA and 205 strikeouts in 178.1 innings.

SP Simeon Woods Richardson: -$10.7 million

The Twins could have challenged for a top-10 spot in these rankings with a healthy Pablo López in the starting rotation. He missed the entire 2026 season recovering from UCL repair surgery with an internal brace and carries a $21.75 million payroll salary for 2027, the final year of his contract.

On a roster loaded with high-profile veteran talent, outfielder Andy Pages and left-hander Justin Wrobleski were first-time All-Star selections and key contributors to a 100-win NL West champion. With all of his deferred money, Shohei Ohtani carried a $2 million cash salary in 2026, which helped keep him atop the best value list.

In the first season of his four-year, $240 million contract, and with a $55 million cash hit on the books, Kyle Tucker was a drain on the Dodgers' bottom line. He hit .233/.330/.385 for a 97 OPS+ with 17 home runs, 70 RBI and 0.7 WAR in 154 games.

The five players listed above represent the present and future offensive core of the Cardinals, and they racked up 17.1 WAR with four of them earning less than $800,000 and Alec Burleson the highest-paid of the bunch with a $3.3 million salary.

While several young players stepped forward with breakout seasons, Matthew Liberatore (31 GS, 5.23 ERA, 155.0 IP, -0.6 WAR) and Nolan Gorman (85 G, 66 OPS+, .184 BA, -0.3 WAR) failed to take a developmental step forward. Both players are arbitration-eligible this winter and look like potential non-tender candidates.

CJ Abrams and James Wood combined for 63 home runs and 8.8 WAR while earning just over $5 million total, helping to make the Nationals one of the highest-scoring offenses in baseball. An equally big takeaway was the breakout performance of a finally healthy Cade Cavalli, who earned himself a four-year, $47 million extension.

Miles Mikolas (5.82 ERA, 116.0 IP) and Zack Littell (4.97 ERA, 112.1 IP) ate innings at a relatively low cost, and while the returns were lacking, there is value in absorbing some of the workload on a young staff. The Nationals have done a solid job keeping bad contracts off the books since the Patrick Corbin and Stephen Strasburg deals.

Brandon Lowe, Mason Montgomery (+$18.4M) and Jake Mangum (+$6.4M) were all acquired from the Rays in the three-team trade that sent Mike Burrows (-$8.6M) to the Astros—arguably the most successful deal of the 2025-26 offseason. Lowe is now a free agent, but Montgomery has emerged as the closer of the present and future.

For a team that doesn't spend big, Marcell Ozuna (67 OPS+, 8 HR, -1.0 WAR) proved to be a disastrous addition on a one-year, $10.5 million deal that will also cost them a $1.5 million buyout on a 2027 option. On a positive note, that money is now off the books and available for further additions this winter.

Caleb Durbin, Sonny Gray and Willson Contreras were all offseason additions via trade to the Red Sox roster, and all three were 4-WAR players for a team that navigated significant injuries to reach the postseason. The two incumbents, Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela, bolstered their tremendous value with Gold Glove defense.

After a healthy, bounce-back season in 2025, Trevor Story struggled through yet another injury-plagued season. In the 64 games he did play, he posted a 75 OPS+ and 0.2 WAR, and his absence and lack of production created a significant hole at shortstop for much of the year. Will he be pushed to the side by top prospect Franklin Arias in 2027?

With 9.1 WAR and just $1.6 million in combined salary, the double-play tandem of Xavier Edwards and Otto Lopez went a long way in vaulting the Marlins into the top five in these rankings. The decision to trade catcher Liam Hicks to Tampa Bay with four years of club control remaining is one the front office might regret.

Pete Fairbanks, Chris Paddack, Leo Jiménez and Christopher Morel are already off the Marlins roster, while Tyler Zuber is a clear non-tender candidate, so the Marlins have a path out from under their five worst values of the 2026 season. The front office has almost completely kept long-term financial commitments off the books, outside of Sandy Alcantara (+$6.2M) who provided positive value.

The White Sox's rise to contention was backed almost entirely by the development of their own in-house talent, with Miguel Vargas, Chase Meidroth, Tristan Peters and Sam Antonacci (+$19.3M) all posting a 110 OPS+ or better en route to a combined 16.0 WAR. Slugger Munetaka Murakami (+$1.4M) was also a net positive in total value.

Andrew Benintendi is entering the final season of his five-year, $75 million deal in 2027, and while he ranked as the worst value, he still posted a .240/.302/.413 line with 24 doubles, 15 home runs and 78 RBI. Trade deadline pickup Luis Castillo is owed $24.15 million in 2027, and he will look to bounce back from struggling to an 8.42 ERA in 31 innings after coming over in a trade with Seattle.

Victor Mesa Jr. and Nick Martinez proved to be two of the best pickups of the 2025-26 offseason, playing a key role in leading the Rays to a World Series appearance. It also speaks to just how valuable Taylor Walls is defensively at shortstop that he hit .222 with a 71 OPS+, yet he was still a 3.5-WAR player on his way to Gold Glove honors.

The two-year, $15 million deal to sign Steven Matz was a rare free agency misstep for the Rays, as he logged a 5.49 ERA and 5.02 FIP in 80.1 innings over 11 starts and 25 relief appearances. He is still owed $7.5 million next season, and his 3.95 ERA after the All-Star break should earn him a shot to bounce back.

Homegrown talent is the lifeblood of the Cleveland organization, and they had three of the best rookies in the American League in Parker Messick, Chase DeLauter and Travis Bazzana (+$21.0M) who all ranked among the best values on the roster. Messick is an AL Cy Young finalist, meaning he will finish no lower than third in the balloting.

Rhys Hoskins slugged 13 home runs and provided some pop after joining the Guardians on a minor league deal, so even the club's worst value was not a complete flop, though he did hit just .179 with a 31.5 percent strikeout rate. This club steers clear of almost all free agency spending, so it's not surprising there are few bad values on the roster.

Brice Turang trailed only Pete Crow-Armstrong (9.8) and Cristopher Sánchez (8.1) with 7.3 WAR in 151 games, posting a 124 OPS+ with 37 doubles, 21 home runs, 100 RBI and 19 steals while again providing elite defense. His net value alongside NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski outpaced the entire roster of 15 teams.

Despite his team-worst value, Christian Yelich was named the first captain in Brewers franchise history in September before helping the team win its first World Series title. He hit .235/.315/.378 with 23 doubles, 12 home runs and 59 RBI during the regular season, and is still on the books for $26 million in 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Ranking Mariners OF Randy Arozarena's Top 5 Landing Spots in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Conventional wisdom holds that this winter's free-agent market lacks standout hitters, but nobody can disagree more than Randy Arozarena.
articles.body:
Conventional wisdom holds that this winter's free-agent market lacks standout hitters, but nobody can disagree more than Randy Arozarena.

In parts of eight seasons as a major leaguer, Arozarena has been a history-making playoff hero, a three-time All-Star and a Rookie of the Year. He's also had six straight seasons with at least 20 home runs and stolen bases.

Moreover, Arozarena's most recent season was his finest. He played in 154 games for the Seattle Mariners and turned in career-bests with a 148 OPS+ and 5.7 rWAR. That was from the right side of the plate, where there's currently a shortage of impact talent in MLB.

Since Arozarena is coming off his age-31 season, he is older than teams prefer free-agent prizes to be. He's also nobody's idea of a good defender in left field. Assuming he rejects the Mariners' qualifying offer, he'll be tied to signing penalties until at least December 1, when the current CBA expires.

Still, projections for Arozarena's next contract are in the nine-figure range. B/R's Tim Kelly is especially bullish, projecting a five-year, $140 million deal for the Cuban native.

Given all this, let's size up Arozarena's best landing spots based on how badly they need him and how much money they have to spend. We'll start with honorable mentions, then count down to the top five.

Definitely Need Him, But the Budget Is a Problem

Arozarena with Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart? That sounds fun! The Reds were also in the bottom five in MLB in rWAR from the outfield and in wRC+ from right-handed hitters, so signing Arozarena would check two major boxes. It's therefore too bad they have never spent more than $64 million on a free agent.

It's 2020, and Cleveland needs power in the outfield. It's 2021, and Cleveland needs power in the outfield. It's 2022, and Cleveland… eh, you get the bit. Alas, this team just doesn't spend in the best of times. It shouldn't be expected to now. Its payroll is already slated to go up in 2027.

The Marlins should be ready to make a move. They definitely need a righty power hitter for a lineup that got only 65 home runs from that side of the plate in 2026. However, this franchise has only ever done a single nine-figure deal with a free agent. That was with José Reyes 15 years ago.

Could Use Him, But Have More Pressing Needs

The left side of the field holds several questions for the Braves, including whether they can do better than Mike Yastrzemski to the left of Michael Harris II. Given their pitching needs, though, a new guy out there is more a bonus than a necessity.

The Cubs stand to lose both Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ to free agency, so they can't straight-up ignore their outfield needs. However, they need starting pitching more than the Braves. Heck, more than anyone .

This is more of a fun fit than a clean fit. The White Sox could use another righty slugger to balance out a lineup that got more power from the left side in 2026. They don't really need an outfielder, though. They're otherwise another team that needs to prioritize the mound.

The Padres used 10 different players in left field this year, which captures the revolving door vibe the position has had for a while now. Starting pitching needs loom large again, though. The Padres can, should and must do better than Joe Musgrove as their ace .

If the Mariners are going to keep Arozarena in the Pacific Northwest, they might have to be prepared to pay extra.

He had a good run with the M's after coming over from the Tampa Bay Rays in July of 2024, but Ryan Divish of The Seattle Times reported that Arozarena was "crushed" when the trade went down. He still lives in the Tampa area and reportedly prefers the East Coast.

Plus, T-Mobile Park isn't exactly a tractor beam for free-agent hitters. While the thing with Cal Raleigh at the World Baseball Classic didn't seem to spiral out of control, it still lingers as a bad memory.

If nothing else, the Mariners can't simply leave Arozarena's shoes unfilled. He was their best hitter this season, particularly from the right side. Of their 65 right-handed homers, 26 came from him.

Payroll-wise, there's a $21 million gap between where the Mariners ended 2026 and where they stand to begin next season. That might be enough for Arozarena, particularly if his QO-related penalties scare other teams off. Obviously, that's not a concern that applies to the Mariners.

Signing Penalty: Third-highest 2027 draft pick

Let's get right to the fundamental flaw with the Orioles as a fit for Arozarena: they're yet another team that primarily needs pitching.

The team is making no secret of this , nor should it be. Orioles starters finished in the back half of MLB with a 4.24 ERA, even with Trevor Rogers, who is now one of the top arms on the open market. With Chris Bassitt also a free agent, they likely need at least two starters.

However, those spots could conceivably be filled via trade. As reported by Andy Kostka of The Baltimore Banner, only Pete Alonso is considered untouchable. That implies even Gunnar Henderson is available. He's just one piece in an overcrowded infield that could prove useful in landing a starter.

Meanwhile, there's a $26 million gap between what the Orioles spent in 2026 and what they project to spend in 2027. That's roughly an Arozarena-sized chunk of change. He would fit nicely in an Orioles outfield that offers little certainty.

More to the point, Arozarena could help Alonso carry the offense. The Orioles badly need a guy like that, as Alonso's 43 home runs this year accounted for 20 percent of the team's total.

Signing Penalty: $1 million in international bonus pool money, second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks

On paper, at least, Arozarena and the Blue Jays are about as obvious as fits get.

They finished last in MLB in scoring this year, so this winter simply can't pass without at least one big bat heading north of the border. They were also tied for last in the league in WAR from left field.

While the Blue Jays should have faith that Vladimir Guerrero Jr. will bounce back in 2027, they would be wise to look around for an insurance policy for the middle of their batting order. Arozarena would fit the bill and then some. Indeed, he's out-homered Guerrero over the last four seasons.

The Blue Jays seem to have as much as $30 million to add to their 2027 payroll, so affordability is not an issue here. The penalties associated with signing Arozarena might be a different story, but emphasis on "might." Ostensible World Series contenders like the Blue Jays should be willing to take such risks.

Instead, a more pressing question might be whether Toronto prefers signing Arozarena. Courtesy of Mitch Bannon of The Athletic , the first outfielder the Blue Jays were connected to after the season ended was actually Seiya Suzuki.

The Red Sox were supposed to add power last winter, but ultimately fell short. It cost them, as scoring runs the hard way didn't do them much good at the back end of the regular season or in the postseason.

Thus, we get this note from Ian Browne of MLB.com: "Boston's top need is another right-handed-hitting thumper to go with Willson Contreras."

Sounds about right, and that note was unsurprisingly part of a blurb about Arozarena as a fit for the Red Sox. He's certainly no stranger to Fenway Park. There's nothing wrong with his .833 OPS in 32 career games there.

That said, there is a "buyer beware" element here. Arozarena's bat speed is trending down. His rate of pulled balls in the air is on the same trajectory. As such, he might not be an ideal fit to take aim at the Green Monster.

Money is another question mark here. The Red Sox just don't spend in free agency like they used to. They're already projected for a higher payroll in 2027 than the one they had in 2026. How aggressive they're willing to be on the open market is an open question.

The Phillies need to shake up their roster this winter. They'd be wise to be ruthless about it. It should be as much about who should go as about who should come.

That said, take a look at these stats from 2026 and see if you can see why Arozarena should appeal to the Phillies:

Clearly, Arozarena is about as "two birds, one stone" a free agent target as the Phillies could ask for. His swing arguably fits better at Citizens Bank Park than it would even at Fenway Park. Per Statcast, he would have hit 25 home runs in Philly this year, compared to just 16 in Boston.

Unlike the Red Sox, the Phillies' projected 2027 payroll is currently short of their 2026 spending level by $20 million . Given that and all of the above, it's no surprise to hear Jim Bowden of The Athletic say that Arozarena is "on their radar."

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Japanese Phenom Shoki Oda Linked to Yankees, Dodgers, Phillies, Rangers in New MLB Rumors
articles.summary: With 18-year-old pitching phenom Shoki Oda eyeing an immediate move to MLB rather than starting his pro career in his native Japan, several clubs have been linked to the right-hander.
articles.body:
With 18-year-old pitching phenom Shoki Oda eyeing an immediate move to MLB rather than starting his pro career in his native Japan, several clubs have been linked to the right-hander.

Per MLB insider Francys Romero , Oda is expected to meet with the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies, among others, ahead of him potentially being eligible to sign when the international signing period opens on Jan. 15.

Romero also reported the eight officials from the Texas Rangers met with Oda this week that "left a great impression" on the teen phenom.

Oda does appear to have a favorite among the potential interested teams if the choice is left up to him.

Dylan Hernandez of the New York Post noted Oda's favorite player is Yoshinobu Yamamoto and the only MLB club he follows on Instagram is the Dodgers.

Oda announced on Oct. 15 he intends to move to the United States to pursue his baseball career rather than enter the NPB draft. He included college baseball among his options if he were to go unsigned by MLB teams.

This is becoming a growing trend among Japanese-born players in order to get into MLB at a younger age.

Rintaro Sasaki, who set the high school home run record in Japan, opted to sign with the Miami Marlins after being selected in the eighth round of the 2026 draft. He had previously been a first-round pick by the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks in the NPB draft in October 2025.

Shotaro Morii signed with the Athletics as an international free agent in January 2025. Genei Sato will pitch for Penn State next season to be eligible for the 2027 MLB draft after transferring from Sendai University.

Oda, who pitched for Yokohama High School, has a fastball that has touched the high-90s already.

One potential wrinkle in Oda's immediate MLB plan is it's unclear if there will be an international signing period in January.

The league and MLB Players Association have until 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 before the current CBA expires, which would lead to a lockout and freeze on all business.

It's also unclear what free agency for international players will look like under a new CBA because MLB has been proposing an international draft as part of its labor talks.

Under the current system, Oda would be subject to international signing rules and teams could only offer him a deal based on their allotted bonus money.

articles.summary: The best hitters in baseball are one step closer to being honored for their contributions during the 2026 MLB season.
articles.body:
The best hitters in baseball are one step closer to being honored for their contributions during the 2026 MLB season.

Louisville Slugger announced the finalists at each position for the Silver Slugger. The group is headlined by MVP candidates Pete Crow-Armstrong and Yordan Alvarez along with Shohei Ohtani, Pete Alonso, Bobby Witt Jr., Mike Trout and Fernando Tatis Jr.

The Silver Slugger winners will be revealed on Nov. 17. They're the last of the season awards to be distributed.
